title: Adaptive staging buffers and threadpool revamp to cut CPU-GPU overhead
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Goal: reduce end-to-end host CPU and memcpy overhead during prefill and decode paths for short-to-medium sequence workloads by redesigning buffer staging, eliminating redundant copies, and making the host threadpool adaptive to live workload shapes.

Problem summary: In the current host->GPU pipeline we see three dominant sources of overhead for production text workloads: (1) bursty memcpy spikes from per-request staging buffers that cause CPU stalls and NUMA imbalance; (2) excessive scheduling contention on a fixed-size threadpool when many low-latency requests arrive concurrently (canary tests show up to 40% CPU spent in thread synchronization at peak); (3) suboptimal kernel choices forcing extra host-side reshapes/prefix-copies for attention kernels with mixed sequence lengths.

Approach: Implement a combined runtime change with three coordinated components: 1) DMA-friendly ring of pinned staging buffers with scatter-gather descriptors to let the GPU DMA engine pull directly where supported, avoiding an intermediate user-copy per request; 2) adaptive host threadpool that dynamically scales and switches between cooperative work-stealing and lockless SPSC lanes depending on concurrency and request size distributions; 3) kernel selection advisory that exposes a lightweight per-model hint to avoid host reshapes by selecting attention kernels tolerant of ragged sequence lengths or by precomputing packed-layouts in the pinned buffer.

Key design decisions and trade-offs: we prefer a single shared pinned-ring over per-stream pinned buffers to reduce kernel argument churn and page pin refcounts; this adds complexity for lifetime tracking and requires a tighter backpressure policy. The adaptive threadpool will default to conservative sizing to avoid regressing tail latency for single-request flows; we accept slightly higher peak idle CPU to massively reduce contention under load. Kernel-advisory is non-invasive: model onboarding supplies an optional hint, and we provide a fallback path to current kernels to preserve correctness.

Telemetry and measurement plan: add per-request host_time breakdown (staging_copy_us, queue_wait_us, thread_lock_us, kernel_selection_us) and a memcopy-byte counter sampled per-second. Baseline synthetic microbenchmarks (gpt-medium, seq_lengths 8/32/128, qps sweep 5->500) showed host_time median 2.6ms with memcpy peaks at 9GB/s. Local experiments with prototype reduced host_time median to 1.0ms and memcpy peaks to 4.7GB/s for the 8/32 mix. We will run 2-week canaries on a subset of routed traffic (5% of production) and compare cost/latency and error rates.

Rollout plan: feature gating behind runtime flag kernel_advisory + pinned_ring + adaptive_pool. Canary rollout in three stages: internal canary (CI cluster) -> 5% production traffic -> 25% with a/b comparison for CPU, tail P99, and request error delta. If CPU drops by >=40% and tail latency improves or stays within 5% of baseline, expand to 100%.

Migration and compatibility: existing Dedicated/private customers remain on current flags until they opt-in. We will provide a migration doc for on-prem operators describing kernel hinting and required kernel library versions.

Risks: DMA support is platform-dependent (cloud drivers/NICs/GPUs). Failing DMA gracefully requires a fallback to the zero-copy host path which may reintroduce copies if drivers are unavailable. Threadpool heuristics could oscillate on pathological workloads; we will implement dampening and rollout it slowly.

Next steps: finish implementation of pinned-ring lifetime manager, wire telemetry counters, add unit+stress tests, open PR for adaptive threadpool shim, and schedule canary.
